title: Why Is the Second Time Faster?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Is the Second Time Faster?' over a small GOLD clone. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP (shared by both films, take-homes and text): V segments BLUE, D segments GREEN, J segments ORANGE; ordinary lymphocytes GREY circles; the selected clone GOLD; memory cells GOLD with a dark outline; antibody in plasma a PURPLE bar; antigen a small RED spiky shape. Every number appears only as on-screen text. No molecular structures: cells are circles, receptors are simple notched shapes, DNA is a row of labelled cards. New here: a dashed BLACK line marks 'enough cells to control the infection' (schematic).

scenes.tts: Suppose an infection leaves you a thousand times more cells that fit a virus. Is your second response a thousand times faster?
scenes.visual: Two GOLD clusters: a tiny one labelled 'before' and a big one labelled 'after: x 1,000 (illustrative)'. A stopwatch beside the big one shows a question mark and '1,000 x faster?'.
scenes.narration: Suppose an infection leaves you a thousand times more cells that fit a virus. Is your second response a thousand times faster?

scenes.tts: The first film ended with an antigen choosing the few cells that fit. But a few cells cannot fight an infection. How do a few become enough?
scenes.visual: Brief replay from the first film: the RED antigen docks on one cell, which turns GOLD among GREY cells. A huge swarm of RED virus particles appears beside the single GOLD cell, labelled 'not enough'.
scenes.narration: The first film ended with an antigen choosing the few cells that fit. But a few cells cannot fight an infection. How do a few become enough?

scenes.tts: A chosen cell divides into two. Each of those divides again. With every round of division, the clone doubles.
scenes.visual: One GOLD cell splits: counters read '1', '2', '4', '8', '16', '32' as the cluster grows round by round.
scenes.narration: A chosen cell divides into two. Each of those divides again. With every round of division, the clone doubles.

scenes.tts: So the number of cells is the starting number, doubled once for every round. Enough rounds turn a few cells into millions.
scenes.visual: The rule writes itself on screen: 'cells = starting cells x 2^n', with 'n = number of doublings' underneath. The cluster keeps doubling into a dense GOLD crowd.
scenes.narration: So the number of cells is the starting number, doubled once for every round. Enough rounds turn a few cells into millions.

scenes.tts: Now draw it as a graph. Days run along the bottom. Cell number runs up the side. Each gridline is ten times the one below.
scenes.visual: Axes draw in: x axis 'days', y axis 'fitting cells' on a log scale with gridlines labelled '10', '100', '1,000' and up to '10,000,000'. The dashed BLACK line 'enough cells (schematic)' sits high on the axis.
scenes.narration: Now draw it as a graph. Days run along the bottom. Cell number runs up the side. Each gridline is ten times the one below.

scenes.tts: On this axis, steady doubling is a straight climb. A first response starts from a few cells, so it needs many doublings. It takes days to build.
scenes.visual: A computed GOLD curve: flat for a short lag, then a straight climb from about '100 cells (illustrative)' to the dashed line. A bracket along the climb reads 'about 17 doublings (computed, illustrative)'. Caption 'primary response'.
scenes.narration: On this axis, steady doubling is a straight climb. A first response starts from a few cells, so it needs many doublings. It takes days to build.

scenes.tts: When the infection is cleared, most of the expanded cells die. But memory B cells and memory T cells remain. There are many more of them than the clone started with.
scenes.visual: The GOLD curve peaks, then falls steeply, labelled 'most cells die'. It levels off into a plateau of dark-outlined GOLD memory cells, labelled 'memory', far above the starting '100' gridline.
scenes.narration: When the infection is cleared, most of the expanded cells die. But memory B cells and memory T cells remain. There are many more of them than the clone started with.

scenes.tts: Suppose the memory pool is a thousand times bigger than the starting clone. How many fewer doublings does a second response need?
scenes.visual: A bracket between the starting level and the memory plateau, labelled 'x 1,000 (illustrative)'. A question card: 'how many fewer doublings?'
scenes.narration: Suppose the memory pool is a thousand times bigger than the starting clone. How many fewer doublings does a second response need?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: About ten fewer. A thousandfold head start covers only about ten doublings. So it saves those rounds, not a thousandfold of the time.
scenes.visual: On screen: '2^10 = 1,024, about 1,000', so 'x 1,000 = about 10 doublings'. The doubling stair from the first curve is shown with its first ten steps shaded and labelled 'skipped'.
scenes.narration: About ten fewer. A thousandfold head start covers only about ten doublings. So it saves those rounds, not a thousandfold of the time.

scenes.tts: So the second curve starts high and reaches the line sooner. This second, secondary response needs fewer rounds of division. Real secondary responses are usually larger too, for reasons this simple model leaves out.
scenes.visual: A second computed GOLD curve starts from the memory plateau, climbs with the same slope and crosses the dashed line well before the first curve did. Labels: 'primary' and 'secondary'; a gap between the two crossing points labelled 'fewer doublings'. No claim about peak height is drawn from this model.
scenes.narration: So the second curve starts high and reaches the line sooner. This second, secondary response needs fewer rounds of division. Real secondary responses are usually larger too, for reasons this simple model leaves out.

scenes.tts: This doubling picture is a simplified model. It leaves out cell death during the climb. And many memory cells, though not all kinds, respond faster than first-time cells.
scenes.visual: A small tag 'simplified model' pins to the graph. Two notes slide in beside it: 'leaves out: cells dying during expansion' and 'leaves out: many memory cells respond faster than naive cells (varies by memory subset)'.
scenes.narration: This doubling picture is a simplified model. It leaves out cell death during the climb. And many memory cells, though not all kinds, respond faster than first-time cells.

scenes.tts: Where does a head start come from? Compare two mice. One gets a harmless viral protein, as a vaccine. Its own fitting cells expand, and memory cells stay behind.
scenes.visual: Two mouse cartoons side by side. Left mouse labelled 'gets viral protein (vaccine)': a small GOLD clone inside grows, shrinks, and leaves dark-outlined GOLD memory cells.
scenes.narration: Where does a head start come from? Compare two mice. One gets a harmless viral protein, as a vaccine. Its own fitting cells expand, and memory cells stay behind.

scenes.tts: The other mouse gets antibody taken from an immunized mouse. It is protected at once. But the antibody is broken down, and no memory cells were made.
scenes.visual: Right mouse labelled 'gets antibody from an immunized mouse': a PURPLE antibody bar appears full at once, then shrinks over a timeline labelled 'weeks'. No GOLD cells appear inside it.
scenes.narration: The other mouse gets antibody taken from an immunized mouse. It is protected at once. But the antibody is broken down, and no memory cells were made.

scenes.tts: Protection your own lymphocytes make is active immunity. Protection by antibody from another body is passive immunity.
scenes.visual: Labels drop onto the mice: left 'active immunity: your own cells, leaves memory'; right 'passive immunity: borrowed antibody, no memory'.
scenes.narration: Protection your own lymphocytes make is active immunity. Protection by antibody from another body is passive immunity.

scenes.tts: Six months later, both meet the virus. The vaccinated mouse starts high on the curve. The other starts from the bottom, like a mouse that never met it.
scenes.visual: Each mouse gets a mini graph: the left one's GOLD curve starts from a memory plateau and reaches the dashed line early; the right one's starts at the naive level and climbs the full way. Caption 'six months later'.
scenes.narration: Six months later, both meet the virus. The vaccinated mouse starts high on the curve. The other starts from the bottom, like a mouse that never met it.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'Memory is a head start: fewer doublings to enough cells.'
